strengths: The paper targets a genuinely under-explored evaluation setting: fine-grained visual reasoning over information-dense, high-resolution structured diagrams (transit maps). This complements existing abstract-puzzle (VisualPuzzles, VGRP-Bench) and domain-specific (CityBench, MapEval) benchmarks, and the gap is well motivated in the related work and Table 1.

The dataset construction pipeline is described in reasonable detail: semi-automated line/stop extraction with manual correction, template-based question generation, reference routes collected from map-service APIs, and explicit quality control covering correctness, diversity, and difficulty balance. The design is extensible, as claimed.

The two-level evaluation framework (binary correctness plus a graded 'map score' that credits route segments, endpoints, and via-stop accuracy) is a sensible way to give partial credit on route-planning answers, and the scoring algorithms are provided in the appendix.

The model study is reasonably broad (15 models, base and reasoning variants, open- and closed-source) and includes an informative text-only ablation (Table 3) that quantifies reliance on parametric knowledge versus visual input, revealing that some open-source models even improve without images — a useful and honest negative finding.

The paper is well organized and transparent about experimental setup, difficulty-aware weighting, image preprocessing differences across models, licensing, and ethical considerations; supplementary case analyses are concrete and illustrative.
weaknesses: Limited task diversity: all questions come from essentially three templates (short route, long route with via-stop count, long route with via-stop enumeration). The benchmark therefore measures a fairly narrow slice of 'fine-grained visual reasoning', and the claim of broad assessment of spatial reasoning is overstated relative to this narrowness.

Small and potentially noisy evaluation set: only 312 test samples, with some difficulty buckets containing very few examples (e.g., 1 sample for hard-middle, 7 for hard-easy). Figure 3's per-bucket accuracies on such buckets are statistically fragile, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the headline comparisons (e.g., base > reasoning among open-source models).

A validity concern about reference routes: routes are obtained from Gaode/Google Map APIs, which operate on real geographic data, while the models must reason over stylized, non-geographic transit map images. The paper discards routes that 'cannot be visually traced on the map', but the notion of a single 'optimal' route is fragile; the correctness check only verifies internal consistency with Map Metadata (route/stop existence and transfer continuity), not actual optimality, so alternative valid optimal routes not returned by the API could be unfairly penalized in the map score.

Knowledge leakage is acknowledged but only partially mitigated: Table 3 shows models like Qwen2.5-VL-3B scoring better without visual input, meaning a nontrivial portion of the benchmark is answerable from prior knowledge of well-known metro systems. No de-contamination mechanism (e.g., synthetic or renamed stops) is offered.

The map score involves several heuristic design choices (point caps, bonus of 10/20 for correct answers, ad hoc via-stop error mapping, difficulty weight matrix) whose impact on model rankings is not ablated; rankings under plain unweighted accuracy are not reported alongside the weighted results.

The headline finding (open-source reasoning models underperform their base variants) rests on a small number of model pairs and small test set, and the explanation offered (RL-induced bias, limited visual grounding) is speculative without supporting analysis such as per-sample paired comparisons.

Closed-source API results are subject to version drift and undisclosed serving configurations; the paper itself footnotes that cross-model comparison in this group may be unfair, which weakens conclusions drawn from those numbers.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine gap: existing multimodal reasoning benchmarks (MathVerse, VisualLogic, VGRP-Bench, V*-Bench) do not systematically evaluate fine-grained perception and multi-step spatial reasoning on dense, information-rich diagrams, and high-resolution transit maps are a well-motivated testbed for this.

The dataset construction pipeline is documented in reasonable detail (semi-automated line/stop extraction with manual correction, API-based reference route collection, discard rules for routes not visually traceable, difficulty quotas), and the appendix provides question templates, map sources, evaluation algorithms, and license/consent information, which supports reproducibility.

The two-level evaluation (binary correctness plus a graded map score rewarding route segment overlap, endpoint consistency, and via-stop accuracy) is more informative than pure exact-match accuracy and is fully specified in Algorithm 2.

The study covers 15 models spanning base and reasoning variants and open- vs. closed-source, and includes a text-only (masked visual input) control, which is the right experimental design for probing visual grounding versus prior knowledge.

The headline findings are interesting and clearly reported: open-source reasoning models underperform their base counterparts while the opposite holds for closed-source models; several open-source models maintain or improve performance without visual input, exposing reliance on memorized transit knowledge.
weaknesses: The core claim that REASONMAP measures 'fine-grained visual reasoning' is weakened by the paper's own evidence: in Table 3, text-only performance is close to, or better than, full-input performance for several models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B's weighted map score for long questions rises from 5.68 to 6.49 without the image). A substantial fraction of the benchmark appears solvable from parametric knowledge of real transit systems, so the metric conflates memorized route knowledge with visual perception. The authors acknowledge this but do not quantify or mitigate it (e.g., by filtering questions answerable without vision or reporting a vision-dependent subset).

Task diversity is very narrow: only three fixed question templates (one short, two long) all of the form 'how do I get from stop 1 to stop 2', generated by randomly sampling stop pairs. With 1,008 QA pairs over essentially one question schema, the benchmark risks rewarding template-following behavior rather than broad spatial reasoning, and models can be trivially tuned to the required output format.

Ground-truth validity is a concern. Reference routes come from Google/Gaode routing APIs, which optimize real-world travel (schedules, entrances, service patterns), not the topology depicted in the schematic map image. The correctness check (Algorithm 1) is binary over the API route, so a model that produces a genuinely valid, visually traceable alternative route of equal length is scored incorrect. Similarly, 'optimal route' is never defined formally relative to the map graph, making the accuracy metric potentially unfair and the map score's route-matching components noisy.

The map score design is ad hoc: point values (2 for route name, 1 per endpoint, caps at 10/20, a +10/+20 correctness bonus, averaging IoU with exact match count) and the difficulty-weighting matrix in Appendix B.2 are justified only by intuition ('moderate differences... to preserve evaluation stability'). No sensitivity analysis or validation against human judgment of answer quality is provided.

Difficulty labels are subjective: map difficulty is manually assigned to three levels by the authors, and question difficulty is defined solely by transfer count. No inter-annotator agreement, annotation guidelines, or validation that these labels correlate with observed model or human difficulty is reported.

The evaluation set is small: only 312 test samples (with difficulty buckets as small as 1 sample, e.g., hard-middle per Figure 3), which makes the fine-grained difficulty analyses and the open-vs-closed-source 'counterintuitive' conclusion statistically fragile. The finding rests on a handful of reasoning model variants (3 open-source, 4 closed-source), and confounds such as prompt formatting, image preprocessing (noted in Table A2), and token budgets are not controlled.

The annotation pipeline uses MLLMs to extract line/stop metadata followed by manual correction, but the extent of human verification (who, how many annotators, error rates found, disagreement resolution) is not reported, making data quality difficult to assess.

Presentation issues: Figure 1 is cluttered and hard to parse; 'Weighted Acc.' is used in Table 2 before the weighting scheme is introduced in Section 5.1; and Table 1's dataset-size column mixes incomparable units (raw counts vs. multiplied variants), complicating the intended comparison with prior benchmarks.

strengths: Well-motivated gap: existing multimodal reasoning benchmarks (MathVQA, MMMU, VisualLogic, V*, etc.) do not target fine-grained spatial reasoning over dense, information-rich real-world diagrams; high-resolution transit maps are a sensible and underexplored testbed, and the paper positions this clearly against prior map-based work (CityBench, MapEval, GeoNav) that relies on tool/API assistance rather than genuine visual reasoning.

Reasonable dataset construction effort: 1,008 human-verified QA pairs over 30 high-resolution maps from 30 cities/13 countries, with a documented semi-automated pipeline (map metadata extraction with MLLM assistance plus manual correction, template-based question generation, reference route collection, human quality control), difficulty labels at both map and question level, and a held-out 312-sample test split. Map sources and licensing are documented in the appendix.

The two-level evaluation framework (rule-based correctness check via Algorithm 1, plus a fine-grained 'map score' that credits partial route components and via-stop accuracy) is a thoughtful design that goes beyond binary accuracy and enables partial-credit analysis of long-form route answers.

Comprehensive empirical study: 15 MLLMs including both base and reasoning variants, with token-cost reporting, difficulty-aware weighting, difficulty-bucket analysis, per-city analysis, and a well-designed no-visual-input ablation that quantifies reliance on internal knowledge priors. The counterintuitive finding that open-source reasoning variants underperform their base models while the opposite holds for closed-source models is genuinely interesting and connected to prior RL literature.
Qualitative error analysis is informative, categorizing failures into visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, and refusal, with concrete examples in the main text and appendix.

Good reproducibility posture: inference settings specified, official model configurations followed, code released under MIT license, map source links and model licenses provided, and limitations/broader impact explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Ground-truth validity is the most material concern. Reference routes are obtained from Gaode/Google Maps routing APIs, which optimize using real-world schedules and travel times rather than the topology of the printed transit map. Thus the 'one optimal route' a question demands may not be derivable from the visual input alone, and a model that reads the map correctly could produce a different valid route. The correctness check (Algorithm 1) only verifies feasibility (route names exist, stops valid, transfers consistent), not optimality, creating a mismatch between the question wording and the metric; the map score then penalizes answers against API-derived references. The paper does not report how often multiple distinct feasible routes exist per query or how such conflicts were adjudicated.

Question diversity is narrow: essentially one underlying task (point-to-point routing) instantiated through only three templates, with questions randomized over stop pairs. This limits the benchmark's coverage of 'fine-grained visual reasoning' more broadly and risks models exploiting template regularities.

The test set is small (312 samples), and difficulty is highly imbalanced (181 easy / 108 medium / 23 hard; only 7.8% hard overall). Several difficulty buckets contain very few or single samples (e.g., hard-middle has 1 sample, and the paper notes this yields a spurious 100% accuracy), undermining statistical reliability of per-bucket conclusions. No significance testing or variance analysis is provided.

The scoring/weighting design is somewhat ad hoc: the difficulty-aware weight matrix, the cap values (10/20), and the bonus of +10/+20 for answers deemed correct appear hand-tuned without sensitivity analysis or justification, and the map score's composition (segment points, via-stop IoU averaged with exact match counts, then bonuses) makes cross-paper comparability difficult.

The open-source vs. closed-source comparison is acknowledged in a footnote to be potentially unfair (different scales, unknown training data), yet the 'counterintuitive pattern' is presented as a headline finding; the base-vs-reasoning comparison also conflates model size, family, and training recipe differences.

Difficulty labeling for maps is purely manual and the criteria are not operationalized; question difficulty is a proxy (number of transfers), which may not reflect visual difficulty (e.g., dense vs. sparse maps, label clutter, language of stop names).

The finding that models retain performance without visual input partly reflects contamination by world knowledge about well-known metro systems; the paper observes this but does not quantify or control for it (e.g., stratifying by city prominence), which weakens the interpretation of the full-input results.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and underexplored gap: benchmarks combining fine-grained visual perception with spatial route planning over information-dense, high-resolution visual artifacts. The comparison table (Table 1) credibly positions ReasonMap against related benchmarks (V*Bench, MapBench, MapEval, etc.) along useful axes such as resolution, training set, and step evaluation.

The dataset construction pipeline is careful and transparent: MLLM-assisted line/stop extraction with manual correction, reference routes from Google/Gaode Maps with visual traceability filtering, difficulty labeling, and a documented quality-control process (three expert reviewers found and fixed a ~16% error rate). The release of map sources and code is commendable for reproducibility.

The two-level evaluation framework (rule-based correctness plus a decomposed 'map score' covering route name, endpoints, via stops, and IoU) is well specified via Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2, and the authors provide a sensitivity analysis over scoring weights (Table A4) showing rankings are stable — a good practice many benchmarks lack.

The experimental study is broad (16 models spanning open/closed and base/reasoning) and goes beyond headline numbers: visual-masking experiments, symbolic (textualized) map baselines, a language-prior ablation, difficulty-aware weighting, fine-grained error metrics, and qualitative error taxonomy (visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, refusal).

The counterintuitive finding that open-source reasoning variants underperform their base counterparts while the opposite holds for closed-source models is interesting and supported by token-usage statistics and case analyses (e.g., the Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking trial-and-verification failure).

The GRPO-based training baseline with accuracy and format rewards, evaluated in a cross-city disjoint setting, provides a useful reference point and demonstrates the benchmark is usable for training, not just evaluation.
weaknesses: Scale and diversity of the benchmark are limited: only 30 map images (10 per difficulty level) yield 1,008 QA pairs, with a test set of just 312 samples generated from only three fixed question templates. With such a small test set and template-restricted questions, differences between models (e.g., 41.15% vs. 43.14%) are likely not statistically significant, and no significance analysis or variance reporting is provided.

The headline 'counterintuitive' finding rests on only three open-source reasoning models (Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking, Skywork-R1V-38B, QvQ-72B-Preview), all of which are known to be relatively weak or preview-stage models, and only three closed-source base/reasoning pairs. The authors themselves footnote that the closed-source comparison 'may not be fair,' which substantially weakens the generality of the claim.

Reference routes are obtained from Google/Gaode Map APIs rather than derived from the map topology itself; the notion of the 'optimal' route may therefore diverge from what is inferable from the image (service-level routing can weight walking time, frequency, etc.), introducing a systematic mismatch risk. The paper mentions discarding routes that cannot be visually traced, but does not quantify how many routes were discarded or how often service routes disagree with map-inferable routes.

Contamination is a real concern for real-world metro maps and famous station names, and the paper's own language ablation (Table A5) yields mixed results (e.g., English renaming *hurts* Kimi-VL and Doubao-115 on Beijing), which complicates the narrative about language priors and internal knowledge and is not deeply analyzed.

The difficulty-aware weighting scheme (weights 1.0–3.0) and the map-score bonus structure (e.g., +10/+20 bonus for correctness, caps at 10/20/40) are somewhat ad hoc; while sensitivity checks are provided, the headline 'Weighted Acc.' metric is nonstandard and complicates comparison with future work.

The max output token limit of 2,048 for open-source models is close to the mean token counts of reasoning models (e.g., QvQ at 1,619 for long questions), raising the possibility that truncated generations unfairly penalize long-CoT open-source models — a potential confound for the central base-vs-reasoning claim that is not analyzed.

Novelty relative to existing map-reasoning work (MapBench, MapEval, MapLM, CityBench) is incremental; the main differentiators are higher resolution and route-planning granularity, and the RL baseline is limited to a single model family (Qwen2.5-VL), leaving the training-baseline contribution thin.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a genuine and underexplored evaluation target: fine-grained visual understanding combined with spatial planning on information-dense, high-resolution transit maps, which is a useful complement to math/logic-centric multimodal reasoning benchmarks.

The dataset construction pipeline is careful and reasonably documented: MLLM-assisted line/stop extraction followed by manual correction, reference-route collection via map services, difficulty labeling, and quality control including an explicitly reported ~16% initial error rate that was corrected by domain experts.

The evaluation methodology is thoughtfully layered: a rule-based correctness check, a decomposed 'map score' capturing answer quality, difficulty-aware weighting, and supporting ablations (visual masking, symbolic/textual map representations, language bias, sensitivity analysis of score weightings). The symbolic-representation ceiling baseline in Appendix C.4 is a nice addition.

Broad model coverage (16 MLLMs, open and closed source), a GRPO-based RL training baseline with cross-city generalization testing, and structured error analysis (visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, refusal) with released code improve reproducibility and usefulness.
weaknesses: The headline 'counterintuitive finding' (open-source reasoning variants underperform base variants) is weakly supported. The comparison is largely unpaired: QvQ-72B, Skywork-R1V-38B, and Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking are not controlled reasoning versions of the strongest base models (e.g., there is no Qwen2.5-VL-72B reasoning counterpart; the only true paired comparison is Kimi-VL-A3B Instruct vs. Thinking, a single data point). Attributing the gap to 'repeated trial-and-verification' and 'weaker visual grounding' is speculative and rests mainly on cherry-picked case studies rather than systematic evidence.

A serious experimental confound undermines this same claim: the max output token limit is set to 2,048 for open-source models, and reasoning models generate on average 645–1,619 tokens (QvQ near the limit). Long-CoT truncation or format-breakdown under truncation would depress reasoning-model accuracy for reasons unrelated to reasoning quality, and the paper does not report truncation rates or a token-budget ablation.

Limited question diversity: only three templates (one short, two long), with a fixed required answer format. Template rigidity inflates format-error effects, enables partial gaming of the benchmark, and limits how far conclusions about 'fine-grained visual reasoning' generalize.

Reference routes are sourced from Google/Gaode Map APIs, and routes 'that cannot be visually traced' are discarded. This couples ground truth to third-party routing services rather than to map-optimal paths; the paper does not quantify how often routing-service answers diverge from what the map itself implies, nor inter-annotator agreement on what counts as the single 'optimal' route. The map score is also capped per-question (10/20/40), so per-item quality granularity is coarse.

Scale is modest for the claims: 30 maps, 1,008 pairs, and a 312-sample test set, with difficulty buckets as small as 1–7 samples (e.g., hard-middle n=1 shown at 100% accuracy in Figure A1), making fine-grained rankings statistically fragile. No significance testing or variance estimates are provided.

Novelty relative to prior map/spatial benchmarks (MapBench, MapEval, MapLM, CityBench, GeoChain) is incremental; the differentiation rests mainly on resolution and joint 'fine-grained + planning' framing, but the planning component itself is shallow (route with transfers), not true multi-step spatial planning.

Difficulty labels are heuristic proxies (line/transfer counts) and the difficulty-aware weighting matrix is ad hoc; while a sensitivity analysis is included, the weighting scheme risks re-ranking models by robustness assumptions rather than measured ability.

Several observations are asserted rather than demonstrated: e.g., 'closed-source reasoning models excel via stronger visual grounding' is inferred from two case figures, and the OCR-vs-ReasonMap non-correlation (Table A7) covers only 9 models and is not analyzed quantitatively.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing multimodal reasoning benchmarks emphasize either abstract/symbolic reasoning (VisuLogic, VGRP-Bench) or coarse spatial tasks (MapBench, CityBench), while REASONMAP jointly requires fine-grained perception (OCR, line tracing) and multi-step spatial planning over high-resolution (avg ~5,839x5,449 px), information-dense artifacts.

The dataset construction pipeline is well designed and documented: MLLM-assisted line/stop extraction with manual correction, reference routes collected via map APIs with consistency filtering, dual difficulty labels, and explicit quality control. The reported ~16% initial error rate that was subsequently corrected shows the authors took annotation quality seriously rather than hiding it.

The two-level evaluation (binary correctness via Algorithm 1 plus a graded map score decomposing route name, endpoints, transfer consistency, and via stops) is more informative than a single accuracy metric, and the authors provide a sensitivity analysis with alternative weighting schemes (Table A4) showing stable rankings.

The evaluation is broad and well-controlled: 16 models across base/reasoning and open/closed categories, visual-masking and text-only controls, symbolic-representation baselines (Table A6), a language-bias ablation (Table A5), and systematic error analysis distinguishing visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, and refusal.

The GRPO training baseline with cross-city splits is a valuable addition that goes beyond pure benchmarking, and consistently improves accuracy and token efficiency across model scales (Table 4), validating the reward design.

Reproducibility is addressed well: code release under MIT license, dataset release under Apache 2.0, map sources listed (Table A1), explicit inference settings, preprocessing comparison across models (Table A2), and an honest LLM-usage statement.
weaknesses: The evaluation set is small and possibly not fully representative: only 30 maps, 312 test samples across 11 cities, and a heavily skewed difficulty distribution (181 easy, 108 medium, 23 hard). The headline 'hard' conclusions are therefore supported by relatively few samples, and some difficulty buckets contain as few as 1-7 samples (Fig. A1), which makes fine-grained claims statistically fragile.

The headline finding (open-source reasoning models underperform base variants) rests on only three open-source reasoning models (Kimi-VL-Thinking, Skywork-R1V, QvQ), and a potentially confounding factor is not fully ruled out: the 2,048-token cap for open-source models. Reasoning models average 600-1,600 output tokens; QvQ-Preview in particular is known for very long thinking traces that may be truncated, which would depress its accuracy and partly explain the pattern. The authors assert 2,048 tokens is 'sufficient' but provide no truncation statistics.

Ground-truth routes are taken from Google/Gaode map services and filtered for visual traceability, but multiple valid routes often exist in transit networks. Correctness requires each predicted segment's route name and stops to exist in Metro Data and transfer consistency, yet it is unclear whether alternative feasible routes are penalized, and whether map-service routes (which may incorporate schedules or closures) truly correspond to the topology depicted in the static map images.

Prior-knowledge contamination is a real threat that is only partially addressed: the text-only experiments (Table 3) and the Beijing/Hangzhou results (Table A5, e.g., Doubao-415 reaching 84.86% on Beijing) show models possess substantial memorized knowledge of real transit systems, meaning performance on some cities reflects memorization rather than visual reasoning. The masking analysis helps, but the benchmark's value as a 'visual reasoning' measure varies by city, and the authors themselves note city prominence effects.

The difficulty-aware weighting scheme (Appendix B.3) is hand-designed with somewhat arbitrary weights (1.0-3.0); while a sensitivity analysis is provided, 'weighted accuracy' is the headline metric and its construction is not independently motivated.

Closed-source model comparisons are admittedly unfair (footnote 1): unknown image preprocessing, API versioning, and possibly map-retrieval-adjacent training data. Doubao variants also appear twice with inconsistent behavior (Doubao-428 underperforms base Doubao-115), complicating the 'reasoning helps closed-source' claim.

Novelty relative to MapBench [77] and MapEval [11] is incremental in construction: the main advances are higher resolution, the two-level metric, and the RL baseline, rather than a fundamentally new task definition. Also, minor presentation issues (e.g., inconsistent city names 'Changshang', some crowding in Figure 3) and the map-score algorithm (Algorithm 2) are difficult to parse and would benefit from a cleaner specification or code-first presentation.

The paper claims benchmark extensibility as a contribution, but scalability of the manual components (16% error correction, route traceability filtering, expert review by only three annotators) is not demonstrated beyond the current 30 cities.
